newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Britain's envoy sees opportunity for Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Britain's envoy sees opportunity for Cyprus.

text.p: Britain's envoy to the Cyprus dispute, Sir David Hannay, said on Tuesday direct talks aimed at a settlement between rival sides on the divided island should be possible before the first half of the year.

Hannay, starting a three day visit to the island -- his fourth since assuming the post last year -- said he hoped this year to persuade those involved of the advantages of achieving a settlement to the decades-old dispute.
"I have recently been in Ankara and in Athens and I found the contacts with the Turkish and Greek governments reasonably encouraging in both cases," Hannay told reporters.

"The governments, like the British government, would like to see early face-to-face negotiations for a comprehensive settlement under UN aegis... We British feel this should be possible before the first half of 1997."
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since Turkey invaded the northern third in 1974 in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time.
Britain, along with Greece and Turkey, is a guarantor power of Cyprus, a former British colony granted independence in 1960.

Turkish Cypriots now live in the north, where they proclaimed a state recognised only by Ankara in 1983. The Greek Cypriot government in the south is internationally recognised as the legitimate government of Cyprus.
The last time the leaders of each side met for talks was in October 1994.

Hannay is the lastest in a small army of mediators assisting the United Nations in its attempts to breach the dispute and reunite Cyprus in a bicommunal bizonal federation in accordance with agreements reached between the two sides in 1977 and 1979.
He dismissed suggestions he was planning on submitting a blueprint solution to both sides.
The British envoy said that during his talks he would cover a range of issues relevant to a comprehensive settlement but declined to be more specific.
But Hannay said the prospect of a settlement was unlikely so long as the constitutional aspects of the dispute remained open.
"This means we have to get into grips with who is making the decision making in a federal government, the allocation of powers...," said Hannay.
On Monday Gustave Feissel, resident representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on the island, started a new round of proximity talks in preparation of direct negotiations.
Hannay said Greek Cypriot plans to purchase anti-aircraft missiles from Russia and reactions had not helped. Turkey warned of military force to block their deployment due next year.

"I think what they have done is make the task of those like myself to try and bring about a settlement a little bit more difficult. But they have also made it quite a lot more important because they've underlined the risks of not reaching a settlement," he said.
